title: I borrowed a trick from epidemiology to investigate AI clones on Steam and I found they’re not as prevalent as we think and they burn out fast
author: randomstate42
selftext:
This is the last of a 3-part analysis I am doing on AI and Steam. It started with an update on an analysis I did back in December 2025 that went a bit viral. The update went live last week and was all about the impact of AI disclosures on sales (you can read that here: [https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-2](https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-2)).

This third and final part I could have never predicted I would be writing about back in late 2025: AI Clones. What strange times we live in.

I basically wanted to ask:

1. Can we detect waves of AI clones on Steam?
2. How prevalent are they?
3. Do the clones win? And how do we avoid our concepts being cloned?

I don’t want to go around accusing people of cloning (I don’t think that achieves anything) so I ask a more specific question:

Are tight clusters of near-identical games exploding onto Steam, very recently, in particular corners of the market? At what rate, and where?

Turns out there is a neat trick from epidemiology called “Kulldorff’s space-time permutation scan”. I could combine this with our “Steam Map” (like a high-dimensional map of steam games that gives the market a “geometry”) to find bursts of very similar concepts in short periods of time which defy random chance that could arise from normal Steam store growth.

This gave me essentially a “Clone Radar” and the results are pretty surprising, especially compared to the discourse online. Yes, the frequency of these clusters of “clones” has increased massive, going from 1 in 450 back in 2025 to 1 in 13-20 now! But, if you look at the share of new store pages falling within one of these “bursts” it is only around 5% of all new store pages being published.

These “bursts” of new highly similar pages also seem to congregate around particular themes. Tidy-up and sorting sims are the most likely to be copied, with 22 bursts totaling 338 pages. Some examples being are

* "Sort Them X" (gnomes, frogs, dogs, alpacas, eggs),
* "Tidy Up Together", whether that’s magic shops, archives, game stores, socks…any kind of “sort the thing” game.

Next are four themes with around 110-135 store pages each:

* Huge-pile incrementals: needle in a haystack, four-leaf clovers, "one million coins", punch or eat your way out of something
* Management sims: niche sports managers, stock trading, etc
* Desktop and taskbar idlers: a tiny shop or pet that lives at the bottom of your screen.
* Strategy and defence games.

Lastly, attention is lopsided with most followers being concentrated in one particular store page (so Steams winner-takes-all economy is no different for these games) and the bursts tend to burn out rapidly. With the trend of pages normally ending in a few weeks.

I could go on and on, but the full analysis is written up here for those interested: [https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-3](https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-3)

I hope this helps alleviate some anxieties around this current issue. I personally think (and hope) it will pass and the trolls that are looking to make a quick buck by cloning peoples games will learn that the gaming economy does not reward this type of behaviour.

comments.author: tworc2
comments.body:
It also doesn't tend to pay for itself. They still need to pay the $100, so a game has to be somewhat enticing for would-be cloners to bother cloning it. And since they're paying for lower quality and obvious cloning, with short-term, fast gains, I'd bet their price is usually much lower.

An unpopular but obvious way to reduce that is to raise the starting cost even further, since it becomes harder and harder for it to become profitable in the amount of time they got.

replies.author: randomstate42
replies.body: I do wonder if steam will increase the cost of listing a game anyway, since they're clearly struggling with the backlog

replies.author: tworc2
replies.body:
I think they will do something to raise the entry barrier in 2027. They probably must, in a business perspective. 

Price is the obvious solution but may have other repercussions... Mainly competition

replies.author: ePi3354
replies.body: As some dev who found the genre at first interesting and created a "clone" in the tidy up genre i thought if you have a story and a twist around it, it would be more then just a clone, it's pretty hard to stand out. I can tell the costs for steam and ai are in but the work time isn't nearly. It takes a lot of time to polish, I would say I've spent nearly 100h just polishing it and still working on improvements.

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body:
Very good write-up. Here are some thoughts (curious about your input), as my game ([Destroy Any Website](https://destroy.spritefusion.com/)) also got cloned since it went viral in October:

1. Cloning is just a thing people do.  
I've passed on negative thinking about having my game being cloned by accepting that it's just a thing people do at diverse degrees. It is just incentives at work: something work, people want to capture a slice of the value. It always been true for anything economically valuable, just now the \_cost\_ of doing so for games is going down by a lot.

2. Depth.  
As said in the write-up, if the game does have deep storytelling, or really well-thought mechanics/game-feel, it will defend better against clones. 100% agree on that. Surprisingly, this is even true for art or technical side. It is easy to clone a verifiable thing, but the clones rarely put the time to taste-pass the results: a tiny detail you think is important will be missing in clones.

3. The problem is not really clones by themselves, but more the noise they create.  
At the end (in my case at least), the clones are full slop things that will fade. So it is not that big of a problem. But the noise they create and the attention they capture can really hurt an indie game I think. Attention is pretty zero-sum, so this is the real challenge I think!

comments.author: max13007
comments.body: I sorta think the wave of slop games will die down just because even the people making them will realize it's too expensive to release on steam compared to the money they'll actually make. I think the number of games released per day/moth whatever will still be much higher than before, but I suspect the avalanche to calm down once they realize there's not really that much money on the table for slop games.

replies.author: CptFlamex
replies.body:
yup , if you spend 2 - 4 months developing a game on a 100-200 dollar sub , you will spend 400-800 dollars MINIMUM on a game , not counting all the other AI services you may use.

Spending 1k +  steams 100 dollars and barely making anything , will cause the wave to die down

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
Cool trick and cool post, thanks for sharing.

I’ve never really understood the clone panicking I see here. Most people aren’t making something worth cloning. Those that are will still have to reach the cloner before they’re at risk. If your idea worth cloning is reaching a cloner, then I have good news for you: you’re almost certainly reaching real people too, which means real people will probably want your game.

The genres most vulnerable to cloning are interesting too. I couldn’t find the non-rude way to explain why they don’t surprise me, so I will keep my comment to myself. :)

Thanks for the post
